craft:Do this one.name: AR Atelier, Gruda
craft:Do this one.teaser: A painter in Konavle raises her own silkworms and teaches the stitch of the valley's costume
craft:Do this one.story: In a stone house at Gruda, at the far end of Konavle, the academic painter Antonia Rusković Radonić keeps silkworms on mulberry leaves from March to November, reels the thread and dyes it, then works it into the tight geometric Konavle embroidery that edges the women's costume worn at Easter. Croatia protects both the silk-making and the embroidery as national heritage. A weekly embroidery circle of local women has met here for more than fifteen years. Visitors are shown the costume collection, then handed cloth, needle and silk to try a pattern of their own. In late October the last silkworms of the season are still feeding.
craft:Do this one.why: The only place on this coast where the whole chain, worm to thread to stitch, sits in one room under one maker.
facts: Watch the silkworms and the reeling, look through the costume collection, then try a Konavle pattern yourself with cloth, needle and silk thread
Half a day was the format of a 2015 group visit; the shop keeps 09:00–12:00 and 17:00–20:00, closed Sunday (In Your Pocket listing, check before going)
No current public price. A 2015 group workshop was EUR 42 a head with a minimum of 20 (Oct 2026 search); ask for a small-group rate
Contact the atelier ahead: we found no open, dated class calendar, so this is a session by request, not a course you enrol in. Silkworms are visible March to November

craft:Other one.name: The Old Town goldsmiths
craft:Other one.teaser: Rečini earrings and puce buttons, still made in workshops inside the walls the way Ragusa wore them
craft:Other one.story: Gold and silver filigree buttons, the puce, once closed the jackets of Ragusan men, and rečini, the drop earrings, were what a bride brought out on feast days. The Dubrovnik Tourist Board names three Old Town workshops that still make this jewellery by the old methods: Vierda, Kraljević and Jurišić. A younger goldsmith, Marko Farac, also works traditional filigree in his own workshop and sells Ston-mussel and coral pieces. You can watch wire become lace through a doorway and buy from the bench. Missing: none of them publishes a class, so you buy, you do not learn.
craft:Other one.why: A pair of rečini bought from the hand that made them is the one Dubrovnik souvenir with five centuries behind it.
facts: Visit the workshops, see filigree being worked, buy direct
Half an hour between the Stradun side streets
Priced by gold or silver weight; no current figures checked
No booking and no class: walk in during shop hours

craft:Other two.name: Deša at Lazareti
craft:Other two.teaser: A women's association weaving and embroidering in the old quarantine halls just past Ploče
craft:Other two.story: Behind the Ploče Gate, in the Lazareti halls above Banje beach, the Deša association sells what its members make: woven bags, silk-embroidered linens, sewn pieces in the patterns of the Dubrovnik coast. It was set up in 2012 to give work to women over forty, women with disabilities and others shut out of the job market, and the money from each sale goes back to them. In 2015 it ran a sampler workshop for a visiting group, where guests got a piece to start themselves. Missing: no single named embroiderer to learn from, and no public class schedule for 2026.
craft:Other two.why: Buy here and the embroidery is real, local, and the money reaches the woman who stitched it.
facts: Buy embroidery and weaving made on site; ask whether a sampler session can be arranged
Shop listed Monday to Friday 08:00–16:00, closed weekends (In Your Pocket, May 2025); Time Out says hours vary, so ring +385 20 42 01 45 first

craft:What is sold as Croatian craft.name: What is sold as Croatian craft
craft:What is sold as Croatian craft.teaser: Much of the embroidery and 'natural' cosmetics on the main street never saw Konavle or a monastery
craft:What is sold as Croatian craft.story: Old Town tourist shops sell embroidery by the stack marked made in Croatia that was never stitched in Konavle: real Konavle work is dense, geometric, in silk, and costs more than the industrial copies beside it. The 'natural' cosmetics shops on Stradun borrow the aura of the city's old monastery pharmacy and sell imported creams packed for visitors. Lace is the other trap: Pag lace comes only from the island of Pag, and Dubrovnik's own historic lace, the point de Raguse, is so thinly documented that scholars still argue over its origin. If a seller cannot say who made a piece and where, assume nobody here did.
craft:What is sold as Croatian craft.why: Ask who made it and in which village; a real maker's shop answers at once.
facts: Turn a piece over: hand embroidery shows knots and small irregular stitches on the back, machine work is flat and even. Ask the seller for the maker's name and village

AR Atelier in Gruda and Deša at Lazareti for embroidery, the Old Town goldsmiths for filigree (each has its own card in this section); the morning market on Gundulićeva poljana sometimes has Konavle pieces

linger:Cogito Coffee.name: Cogito Coffee
linger:Cogito Coffee.teaser: Zagreb's specialty roaster, in an arched passage by the Maritime Museum, with a second bar outside Ploče
linger:Cogito Coffee.story: Cogito started roasting in Zagreb and now pours in Dubrovnik from a small spot on Stajeva, in a vaulted passage near the Maritime Museum at the harbour end of the Old Town, with a few tables outside under the stone. Expect single-origin filter, a properly pulled espresso and a flat white that does not taste of burnt milk. There is a second Cogito just outside the Ploče Gate on Hvarska. Neither is a big room, so it works for an hour of email, not a day's office. Old notes that put Cogito on the Gruž quay could not be confirmed.
linger:Cogito Coffee.why: The best cup inside the walls, before the first cruise tender lands.
facts: Stajeva 5, Old Town (by Pustijerna and the Maritime Museum); second bar at Hvarska 2, outside Ploče
Listed 08:00–20:00 daily (European Coffee Trip, Time Out); In Your Pocket gives shorter off-season hours, 09:00–16:00 and closed Monday until June. Check in winter (Oct 2026)
Single-origin filter or a flat white
For an hour: small room, outdoor tables; plugs and Wi-Fi not confirmed

linger:The ACI Marina lounge.name: ACI Marina Dubrovnik
linger:The ACI Marina lounge.teaser: Up the Rijeka Dubrovačka at Komolac: Wi-Fi, a café bar and a quiet table while the boat is on the pontoon
linger:The ACI Marina lounge.story: ACI Marina Dubrovnik is not in Gruž. It lies at Komolac, about 5 to 6 km up the Rijeka Dubrovačka, the drowned river valley where the Ombla spring rises under the hills and the water stays cold even in August. Around 380 sea berths, open all year. Ashore there is Wi-Fi, a restaurant, a café bar and a pub, a pool, a laundry, a supermarket, a chandlery and an ATM: enough for a crew to do the provisioning list, the charter paperwork and the laundry in one morning. Weekday mornings out of season are quiet.
linger:The ACI Marina lounge.why: The one place near the city where the laundry, the shop, the Wi-Fi and a coffee are all a pontoon's walk apart.

drink:Plavac Mali.name: Plavac Mali
drink:Plavac Mali.teaser: The little blue grape of Pelješac, and a DNA hunt that found Zinfandel's family tree in Dalmatia
drink:Plavac Mali.story: Plavac Mali means little blue, and it is the red of every Dalmatian table. For years Californians, Mike Grgich among the believers, said it was Zinfandel. In 1998 Carole Meredith of UC Davis began testing with Ivan Pejić and Edi Maletić of the University of Zagreb and found it was not the same grape, but related. In December 2001 Pejić brought her a near-extinct vine from Kaštela called Crljenak Kaštelanski: it matched Zinfandel and Primitivo exactly. The team's 2004 paper showed Plavac Mali to be the child of that grape and Dobričić, a variety from the island of Šolta. So Zinfandel is Plavac's parent, not its twin.
drink:Plavac Mali.why: Order it with brodet or lamb from the peka: big, dark, dried-fig fruit and alcohol that often passes 14%.
facts: Deep ruby, dried cherry and fig, firm tannin, high alcohol
Plavac Mali; the top slopes appear as Dingač or Postup, Komarna on the mainland
A Dingač or Postup from Pelješac; EUR 18–120 a bottle (seen May 2026). D'vino pours a flight

sources.label: Wine Spectator, Researchers solve mystery of Zinfandel's origins

drink:Dingač.name: Dingač
drink:Dingač.teaser: Plavac Mali from 45° slopes above the sea, reached through a 400 m tunnel the growers paid for
drink:Dingač.story: Dingač is a strip of near-vertical vineyard between Trstenik and Podobuče on the south face of Pelješac, and in 1961 it became the first protected wine name in Yugoslavia. Growers say the grapes cook three times: from the sun, from the sea's glare and from the white stones. For centuries the harvest came out on donkeys along goat paths. Then the vineyard owners' cooperative borrowed the money and had a 400 m tunnel cut through the ridge from Potomje; it opened on 29 November 1975 and turned a 20 km detour into 4. Today you drive through it, single file, in the dark.
drink:Dingač.why: Drive the Potomje tunnel and come out above the open sea and the steepest vines in Croatia.
facts: Plavac Mali at full ripeness: dark, raisined, warm, often above 14%
Dingač; the neighbouring Postup was protected in 1967
A Dingač from Potomje, EUR 28–80 a bottle (seen May 2026); the Plavac Mali card has the grape's DNA story

sources.label: Croatia Week, How a 400 metre tunnel transformed Croatia's most famous wine region

drink:Pošip.name: Pošip
drink:Pošip.teaser: Korčula's white, from the linked fields of Smokvica and Čara, made for Mali Ston oysters
drink:Pošip.story: Pošip grows almost only on Korčula, in the Smokvica and Čara fields at the centre of the island. Local tradition credits Marin Tomašić of Čara with finding the vine in 1864, and in 1967 it became the first Croatian white given protected status. DNA puts its parents as Bratovina and Zlatarica blatska, two old island grapes. The wine is broad, low in acid, with citrus, almond and a saline finish, usually 13.5 to 14.5%. On this coast it is the bottle opened with oysters on the Mali Ston quay and the lunch white on every boat.
drink:Pošip.why: The white for shellfish: it has the weight to stand next to a flat oyster without disappearing.
facts: Straw gold, citrus peel, almond, salt; soft acidity, 13.5–14.5%
Pošip, often with Smokvica or Čara
Krajančić, Bire, Toreta or the Grgić Pošip; EUR 14–55 a bottle (seen May 2026)

drink:Grk.name: Grk
drink:Grk.teaser: A white that grows only in Lumbarda's sand, from a vine that cannot pollinate itself
drink:Grk.story: Grk means the Greek, and it grows only around Lumbarda, at the eastern tip of Korčula, in sandy soil between the stone walls. Greek settlers from Issa, today's Vis, did found a colony here in the 3rd or 4th century BC, but nobody can prove they brought this vine. The botany is proven: Grk has functionally female flowers, so growers plant Plavac Mali between the rows to pollinate it. Even then the bunches set unevenly and yields are tiny. Fewer than ten estates bottle it. The wine is dry, bitter-almond, saline and herbal.
drink:Grk.why: Taste a vine that needs a red grape beside it to bear fruit at all.
facts: Dry, pale gold, bitter almond, sage, salt
Grk, Lumbarda; Bire and Lumbarda Vina are the names a wine bar is most likely to stock
A single glass at D'vino; EUR 22–48 a bottle (seen May 2026)
The area: under 100 ha in the old guide, under 50 ha in more recent wine writing. The Greek origin of the vine is tradition, not record

sources.label: Reducirana oplodnja cv. Grk (thesis, NSK repository)

drink:Prošek.name: Prošek
drink:Prošek.teaser: Dalmatia's raisin-grape dessert wine, and a fight over its name that Brussels has still not settled
drink:Prošek.story: Prošek is made from grapes left to shrivel, on the vine or on mats in the sun, until the sugar is so dense that the wine stays sweet: amber, raisin, fig and walnut, closer to an old sweet wine than to anything sparkling. When Croatia joined the EU in 2013 it had to drop the name on its labels because Italy said it sounded like Prosecco. Croatia applied again; the Commission published the request in 2021 and received objections from Italy and others. The new EU geographical-indications regulation of 2024 set rules for similar names, but we found no final decision on Prošek as of October 2026.
drink:Prošek.why: Finish a Dalmatian dinner with a small glass; a splash of it also goes into the pašticada marinade.
facts: Amber, sweet, raisin, dried fig, nut
Prošek inside Croatia; on export labels the name is still in dispute
Hectorovich from Hvar or the Saints Hills Prošek; EUR 18–60 a bottle (seen May 2026)
Croatian MEPs say the 2024 regulation allows Prošek's protection; the Commission said the new rules did not decide the case. No final ruling found (Oct 2026)

drink:Travarica and the home rakija.name: Travarica and the home rakija
drink:Travarica and the home rakija.teaser: Herb, grape, green walnut and rose petal: the four bottles a Dubrovnik house keeps
drink:Travarica and the home rakija.story: Before a meal in a Konavle house someone pours travarica: clear grape rakija with sage, rosemary, fennel and immortelle steeped in it, sharp and green. Loza is the plain grape spirit of the coast. Orahovac starts with walnuts picked unripe around St John's Day, 24 June, left forty days or more in rakija with cloves, cinnamon and sugar until it turns dark amber. Rozalin, or rozulin, is the Dubrovnik one: a rose-petal liqueur, made at home, that perfumes the city's rožata custard. Most of the best is never sold; it comes out of an unlabelled bottle.
drink:Travarica and the home rakija.why: Say yes to the unlabelled bottle: home rakija is how a Konavle table says welcome.
facts: Travarica herbal and dry; loza clean grape; orahovac dark, spiced, sweet; rozalin pink-scented
Often none: the best are homemade
Travarica before the meal, orahovac after; EUR 3–6 a pour (seen May 2026)

bars:Buža.name: Buža
bars:Buža.teaser: Duck through a gap in the south sea wall and drink on the rocks with swimmers jumping below
bars:Buža.story: Buža is Dubrovnik dialect for hole, and that is the entrance: a gap in the southern sea wall below the cathedral quarter, signed for cold drinks and the view. Through it, tables and terraces step down the rock toward the open sea, with nothing between you and Lokrum. There are two bars, Buža I and Buža II, run separately. Swimmers drop off the ledges into deep water. There is no food, no running water, no toilet: bottled beer, house white, soft drinks. Bring cash; cards may or may not work. Both run on the weather and the season, and close or cut hours in winter.
bars:Buža.why: Go in the last hour of daylight, when the wall throws its shadow over the rocks and the sea turns metal.
facts: South sea wall of the Old Town, signed from the lanes behind the cathedral; two bars, Buža I and Buža II
Bottled beer, house white, soft drinks; no food
Seasonal and weather-dependent; listings conflict on hours (daylight only vs 08:00–02:00 for Buža II). In late October check on the day. Carry cash

bars:D'vino.name: D'vino
bars:D'vino.teaser: Taste Pelješac and Korčula in one sitting before deciding which cellar to visit
bars:D'vino.story: If the wine boat is not running or the day is too short, D'vino does the tour in glasses: a Plavac Mali flight that sets Grgić, Miloš, Madirazza and Saints Hills side by side, a Pošip flight, and Grk poured singly from Lumbarda. All Croatian, no imports. Go at six and you will know by eight which Dingač to order with dinner.
bars:D'vino.why: One table maps the whole south Dalmatian wine list before you commit to a bottle.
facts: The Plavac Mali flight, then the Pošip flight; a single Grk from Lumbarda
Book the cellar table; the bar is walk-in
EUR 25–55 a head, flights about EUR 15–25 (seen May 2026)
